title: Sauna or Cold Plunge After Strength Training? What Women Who Lift Should Know
description: Cold water immersion can blunt the muscle growth from your lifting session, while sauna use has a more favorable research picture. Here's how to choose based on your goal.
author: Sundee Fundee Team
bestFor: Women who lift and want to know whether a sauna or cold plunge after training helps recovery or works against muscle and strength gains, and how to choose between them based on their current training goal.

sources.title: Cold water immersion attenuates anabolic signaling and skeletal muscle fiber hypertrophy, but not strength gain, following whole-body resistance training
Throwing cold water on muscle growth: A systematic review with meta-analysis of the effects of postexercise cold water immersion on resistance training-induced hypertrophy

body:
You finish a hard lower-body session, and two familiar options are sitting there: the cold plunge tub in the corner of the gym, or the sauna down the hall. Fitness influencers tell you the cold plunge fights inflammation and speeds recovery. Wellness accounts tell you the sauna detoxes you and melts stress. Almost nobody tells you that picking the wrong one, right after you lift, can quietly work against the muscle and strength you are training for.

The research on both is more specific than the marketing around them. Cold water immersion and sauna bathing are not interchangeable "recovery" tools that both just make soreness go away faster. They do different things to your body, on different timelines, and one of them has a real cost if your main goal is building muscle. This guide breaks down what each modality actually does after a strength training session, where the evidence is solid versus thin, and how to build a plan around your goal instead of around whichever one is trending.

## Why the modality you pick should follow your goal, not the trend

Before deciding what to do after your next session, get clear on what you are actually training for right now. Someone chasing hypertrophy during a dedicated growth phase has different priorities than someone managing joint swelling during a heavy competition prep block or trying to fit a second session into the same day. The research below splits cleanly along that line: cold water immersion has a real, repeatable downside for muscle growth, while sauna use has a more consistently positive research picture, with its own set of practical cautions.

## What cold water immersion does to muscle growth

The clearest finding in this space comes from a line of research on post-exercise cold water immersion and resistance training adaptations. A widely cited study published in the Journal of Applied Physiology found that regular cold water immersion after resistance training sessions attenuated anabolic signaling and blunted skeletal muscle fiber hypertrophy over a multi-week training block, even though it did not blunt maximal strength gains in the same lifters.

That finding held up under more scrutiny. A 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis pooled the available trials on post-exercise cold water immersion and resistance training-induced hypertrophy and found a consistent pattern: cooling the muscle down soon after a damaging training bout appears to interfere with the same anabolic signaling pathways, including mTORC1 activity, that drive muscle protein synthesis. The proposed mechanism is that the inflammatory and metabolic stress from a hard set is part of what triggers growth, and dunking that tissue in cold water dampens the very signal you just worked to create.

The practical nuance matters here: strength gains were largely preserved even when hypertrophy was blunted. If your only goal is a heavier one-rep max and you do not care about muscle size, cold water immersion is less clearly a problem. If hypertrophy is part of the goal, which it is for most women following a structured [weekly set target](/blog/weekly-sets-per-muscle-group-women) built around progressive overload, an ice bath taken immediately after a hard lifting session is working against the growth stimulus you just paid for with fatigue.

## When a cold plunge still makes sense

None of this means cold water immersion is always the wrong call. It is a genuinely useful tool in a narrower set of situations:

- **Same-day double sessions.** If you have a second training session, a competition event, or a demanding physical job later the same day, prioritizing how your legs feel in six hours can matter more than long-term hypertrophy from that one session.
- **Multi-day competition or meet weeks.** Managing joint swelling and next-day readiness during a powerlifting meet or a back-to-back training camp is a performance problem, not a hypertrophy problem, and cold exposure is a reasonable tool there.
- **Acute swelling from an aggravated joint.** Localized cold on a specific irritated joint is a different use case than full-body immersion after a normal training session.
- **Off days from lifting.** Using a cold plunge on a rest day, well outside the post-training anabolic window, sidesteps most of the hypertrophy concern entirely.

If none of those apply and you are in a dedicated growth phase, the simplest fix is timing: separate the cold plunge from your lifting session by several hours, or move it to a non-lifting day, rather than skipping it altogether.

## What a sauna does for recovery and cardiovascular health

Sauna bathing has a different, and generally more favorable, research picture. A review of the evidence published in Mayo Clinic Proceedings summarized findings from large observational cohorts showing that more frequent sauna use is associated with a lower risk of cardiovascular disease and all-cause mortality, with proposed mechanisms including improved vascular function, reduced blood pressure over time, and favorable shifts in autonomic nervous system balance. Heat exposure also triggers heat shock proteins, a cellular repair response linked to muscle protein maintenance and stress resilience, though the size and durability of that specific recovery benefit in strength-trained women needs more direct study before treating it as settled.

Unlike cold water immersion, sauna use after training has not been shown to blunt hypertrophy or strength adaptations in the same way. That makes it a lower-risk default for lifters who want a heat-based recovery tool without trading away muscle growth. It is not a substitute for sleep, protein intake, or the training variables that actually drive results, but as an add-on, the evidence leans supportive rather than cautionary.

## Do women respond to heat differently than men do?

This question matters because most foundational thermoregulation research was done on men, and heat guidance built entirely on male physiology does not always transfer cleanly. A study on sex differences in adaptation to intermittent post-exercise sauna bathing, published in Sports Medicine - Open, found that women showed a slower initial adaptive response across the first heat exposures, with comparatively greater early cardiovascular and thermoregulatory strain than men. By around three weeks of consistent post-exercise sauna use, however, women and men showed similar reductions in peak core temperature, skin temperature, and heart rate during a subsequent heat tolerance test.

The practical takeaway is not that sauna use is riskier for women long-term. It is that the first several sessions may feel harder and less comfortable than they will once your body adapts, and that discomfort in week one is not a sign the tool is wrong for you. Build up gradually rather than starting with your longest, hottest session and judging the modality from that single data point.

## A practical protocol for sauna and cold plunge use

Use this as a starting framework, then adjust based on how your body responds and what phase of training you are in.

### If your priority is hypertrophy

- Skip cold water immersion immediately after lifting sessions during dedicated growth blocks.
- If you enjoy a sauna, use it after training or on a separate day; the evidence does not point to the same interference with muscle-building signaling.
- Keep sauna sessions to roughly 15-20 minutes at a time to start, and prioritize rehydration and electrolytes afterward, since heat exposure adds to the fluid loss from the session itself. The guide on [electrolytes for strength training](/blog/electrolytes-strength-training-women) covers how to replace what you lose without overcomplicating it.

### If your priority is same-day or same-week performance

- Cold water immersion is a reasonable tool for managing next-day soreness and joint swelling during meet weeks, tournaments, or unavoidable back-to-back training days.
- Accept the hypertrophy tradeoff as intentional during these short windows rather than a permanent training choice.

### Either way, treat heat and cold as recovery inputs, not recovery replacements

Neither modality replaces the basics that actually drive most of your recovery capacity: adequate sleep, sufficient protein and total calories, and a training week that is not chronically overreaching. If you are already managing a [deload week](/blog/deload-week-programming-strength-training) or noticing that [sleep quality is affecting your training](/blog/sleep-quality-strength-training-gains), fix those variables first. A sauna or cold plunge is a small addition on top of a solid foundation, not a fix for a foundation that is missing.

## Cautions worth taking seriously

Heat exposure is not risk-free for everyone. Pregnant women, people with certain cardiovascular conditions, and anyone prone to fainting or significant blood pressure drops should talk to a clinician before adding regular sauna sessions, and should never push through dizziness, nausea, or chest discomfort during a session. If you already train in hot conditions, layering a sauna session on top of a workout done in [heat](/blog/strength-training-in-the-heat-women) compounds the thermal load for the day, so plan hydration and total heat exposure across the whole day, not just the sauna block. Cold water immersion carries its own cautions for people with cardiovascular conditions or cold sensitivities like Raynaud's phenomenon, and full-body immersion should be approached gradually rather than starting with the coldest, longest exposure available.

## What to do next

If you are in a phase where building muscle is the priority, treat cold water immersion right after lifting as an occasional performance tool rather than a daily recovery habit, and lean toward sauna use or simple passive recovery instead. If you are managing a meet week, a tournament, or an unavoidable double-training day, a cold plunge is a legitimate short-term trade of some hypertrophy signaling for same-day readiness. Either way, give any new heat or cold protocol two to three weeks before judging how your body responds to it, and keep the fundamentals of sleep, nutrition, and sensible programming as the foundation the rest of your recovery plan sits on top of.
